speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROPOSED EXTENSION FOR ONE YEAR FROM
speechtext:
This seems to
me an appropriate moment to direct the attention of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works to the discussion which has been taking place with respect to the rebuilding of the Ottawa city hall. If the government is taking up with the city the renewal of the agreement between the government and the city, I hope my hon. friend will keep in mind the plan of park development which in a general way has been approved by this parliament, and which is in accordance with the views of the federal district commission, as to the improvement of the city, and not permit within a certain area which has been set apart for further park development any rebuilding or extension of existing buildings. The agreement between the city and the government with respect to what is now known as Confederation park contemplated that no rebuilding would take place within the area outlined in the correspondence. Inasmuch as there appears to be a difference of view on the part of some of those concerned with civic affairs with respect to the obligation of the city in the matter, it ought to be made clear by the minister that at least the federal government expects continued cooperation between the city and itself along the lines on which the improvements already made have been undertaken.
To make clearer my meaning, I might say that the previous administration would never have consented to ask parliament for a sum of money sufficient to permit of the expropriation of the old Russell house and Russell theatre and the other buildings in that vicinity and also for the money necessary for the expropriation of the block between Wellington street, Sparks street, Elgin street and the post office, if the object had been simply that of providing a new site for a city hall within a park area. The intention was to create in the heart of the capital of Canada a large central park which would serve the city as well as the capital, because the two are indistinguishable, but which also would have its relation to the whole improvement of the capital. The government was careful in its interviews with the civic authorities at the time to point out that a
scheme of the kind could only be carried out provided there was cordial cooperation between the city and the government. The city undertook to widen Elgin street, to expropriate certain buildings on that street and also to remove certain buildings in the vicinity of the city hall. Part of that undertaking has already been carried out, there are parts which have not as yet been attended to. There is in the correspondence a reference on the part of the city to a conditional approval b3' the citizens. This had reference to expropriations as they might be made from time to time. I understand that with respect to the widening of Elgin street a by-law was submitted which the citizens approved. I understand also that the citizens approved of the tearing down of Knox church and of the expropriation of that property by the city, so that the citizens already have given implied approval of the general scheme of which these particular expropriations form a necessary part.
Since these expropriations were made, as hon. members know, the city hall took fire and was partially destroyed, and at the moment the city fathers are considering whether they should rebuild and make extensions on the existing site or whether they should secure another location and erect elsewhere a new city hall. I hope the government will be firm in having the civic authorities understand that parliament, when it appropriated moneys for the expropriation of the properties mentioned, and the citizens when they approved of the iby-laws for the widening of Elgin street and the expropriation of Knox church, had in mind the general scheme and the undertaking by the city that they would not rebuild in that area, or extend any of the buildings at the time located there, but that as these buildings came down, their sites would become available for the further development of the general park scheme already approved by this parliament and the civic authorities ini office at the time the first expropriations were made.
I am sure that any agreement made by the government with the city, which will appropriately and adequately recognize the obligations of the federal government to -the city, will meet with the general approval of parliament. I do not anticipate any difficulty over the agreement- that may be ultimately reached. I believe, however, that it would be in accordance with the will and the wish of the people of Canada generally that the scheme which has been carefully planned and already considered by the city and by the federal district
City of Ottawa Agreement

commission should be carried out, and this would seem an appropriate moment for the minister to emphasize that point of view in any discussion with the city fathers.

subtopic: PROPOSED EXTENSION FOR ONE YEAR FROM

Yes, the communications were in writing. They set forth what was agreed to in the several interviews between the government, the federal district commission and the city. There is one phrase in the correspondence which, I understand, has given rise at the moment to some comment. It is to the effect that the city will cooperate to the extent to which the taxpayers approve, or something of the kind. Naturally they must have the approval of the taxpayers in whatever they may do. The intention or meaning of that phrase, however, was not that the scheme as a whole should be presented to the taxpayers of Ottawa to be approved by them; it was that as particular by-laws were necessitated under the city's method of procedure, those by-laws would be submitted. Of course, if the by-laws were

defeated, the city would find it impossible to proceed, but as I have said, they did submit a by-law having regard to the widening of Elgin1 street, and a further by-law, I think it was, it may have been one and the same, with regard to the expropriation of the Knox church property. The citizens approved of those by-laws, and at that time the citizens had the whole park scheme before them. So I think, impliedly, the citizens already have given full consent to the general scheme. The one point that was made clear at the time was that no new buildings should be permitted to go up within that area. The city itself, I believe, has to give a licence or some permission to enable any buildings to be erected.

Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 73, to amend the Bankruptcy Act.

Before this bill is read the second time, and inasmuch as it deals in certain respects with conflicting jurisdictions under provincial and dominion statutes, I would take this opportunity of referring the minister to an anomaly in section 121 of the Dominion Bankruptcy Act, dealing with the rights of wage-earners under that statute. Section 121 reads:
Subject to the provisions of section one hundred and twenty-six as to rent, in the distribution of the property of the bankrupt or authorized assignor, there shall be paid, in the following order of priority:-
First, the costs and expenses of the custodian and the fees and expenses of the trustee;
Secondly, the costs of the garnisheeing, attaching, execution or judgment creditor (including sheriff's fees and disbursements) coming within the provisions of subsection one of section twenty-five and subsection three of section twenty-nine;
Thirdly-*
This is the point I want to emphasize: Thirdly, all wages, salaries, commissions or compensation of any clerk, servant, travelling salesman, labourer or workman in respect of services rendered to the bankrupt or assignor during three months before the date of the receiving order or assignment and all indebtedness of the bankrupt or authorized assignor Under any Workmen's Compensation Act;
I would refer the minister to section 125 of the act and suggest that he read it in conjunction with the foregoing. This section reads:
Nothing in the four last preceding sections shall interfere with the collection of any taxes, rates or assessments payable by or levied or imposed upon the debtor or upon any property of the debtor under any law of the dominion, or of the province wherein such property is situate, or in which the debtor resides, nor prejudice or affect any lien or charge in respect of such property created by any such laws.
And now I should like to direct the minister's attention to one of the provisions of the British Columbia Workmen's Compensation Act, which is similar to other compensation acts in the different provinces. Section 46 of the Workmen's Compensation Act of British Columbia, which is similar to practically all of the acts of the different provinces, makes the claim for rates, dues, assessments, and so on, a claim the payment of which is in priority to everything excepting a workman's lien for wages.
Section 143 of the British Columbia Companies Act provides that for three months fMr. Guthrie.]
prior to a seizure wages shall come before a bondholder's claim. There are innumerable instances throughout the statutes where this principle of three months' priority is established, and in this connection I would refer particularly to section 72 of the Dominion Winding Up Act. As the Dominion Bankruptcy Act is now established, there is conflict and uncertainty with regard to wage earners. Judgments of the courts have maintained that the claims allowed by workmen's compensation boards should ibe paid pari pfissu with the claims of the wage earners, but my hon. friend will appreciate that a workman's lien is not always filed in time. The Bankruptcy Act provides that there shall be a stay of proceedings by all creditors once an assignment in bankruptcy has been made or an order declaring bankruptcy has been isued, in which event the workman must go to the court for leave to proceed and often the delay occasioned puts him out of time because the lien must be filed within thirty days of the date of the last work being done.
I suggest to the hon. minister that this is a good time to consider the advisability of amending the present sections of the Bankruptcy Act. My first suggestion is that section 121 should be amended to read as follows:
Subject to the provisions of section 126 as to rent, in the distribution of the property of the bankrupt or the authorized assignor, there shall be paid in priority to any claim for principal or interest, in respect of any mortgage, bond or debenture issue or any other claim whatsoever, all wages, salaries, commissions or compensation of any clerk, servant, travelling salesman, labourer or workman in respect of the services rendered to the bankrupt or assignor during three months immediately preceding the date of the receiving order or assignment, notwithstanding anything in this act to the contrary otherwise provided, and following the payment of the said claims for wages there shall be paid in the following order of priority:
First, the costs and expenses of the custodian and the fees and expenses of the trustee;
Secondly, the costs of the garnisheeing, attaching, execution or judgment creditor (including sheriff's fees and disbursements) coming within the provisions of subsection one of section twenty-five and subsection three of section twenty-nine;
Thirdly, all indebtedness of the bankrupt or authorized assignor under any workmen's compensation act;
Fourthly, claims resulting from injuries to employees of the insolvent debtor to which the provisions of any workmen's compensation act do not apply, but only upon moneys paid or payable to the insolvent estate by persons or companies guaranteeing the insolvent debtor against damages resulting from such injuries.
Section 125 would have to be amended accordingly, to read as follows:
Nothing in the four last preceding sections, except the provision for the payment of three

months' wages, salary, commissions or compensation, as provided in section 121, shall interfere with the collection of any taxes, rates or assessments payable by or levied or imposed upon the debtor or upon any property of the debtor under any law of the dominion, or of the province wherein such property is situate, or in which the debtor resides, nor prejudice or affect any lien or charge in respect of such property created by any such laws.
I refer the minister to a decision in British Columbia in the matter of the Campbell River Mills Limited, in bankruptcy, which has placed the payment of the wage earners' claims behind tihe workmen's compensation board and behind the holders of debentures. My only motive in making these suggestions is to protect absolutely the three months' priority of wage earners, and I would appreciate if the minister would consider the adoption of the proposed amendments.

the intention.

It would
make it that much more difficult for business people to hire money on mortgages. To-day the salaried employees are in a preferred position, which is as it should be, but if they are put still farther ahead I think it would be going just a little bit too far. This matter should have the earnest consideration of the house before we make any sudh move; it should be considered with all [DOT] its obligations, implications and ramifications.

Mr. Speaker, the Bankruptcy Act became law, I think, in 1919, and was put through by the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) when he was Solicitor General. Since that time there have been many amendments and modifications made to the act. There is scarcely an hon. member who practices law who has not at one time or another brought in some little pet amendment of his own and managed to get it through. At present we have three or four amendments of that kind before the house, and this might be an opportune time to have a general revision of the act.
There are nine provinces, each one having its own particular insolvency law. There was a very drastic revision made for the province of Quebec when Sir Lomer Gouin was Minister of Justice, the object being to bring the Bankruptcy Act in line with the Civil Code
and Code of Procedure of that province. We have in the province of Quebec a bankruptcy act which differs from that of the other provinces and with which we are pretty well satisfied. We have gone along now for the last ten or eleven years and there have been many bankruptcies, in fact some of the boards of trade and other finacial institutions think there have been too many. Unfortunately I was the party who first introduced the bankruptcy bill into the house. At that time I think I had more influence with the government than I have to-day because I succeeded in placing it on the doorstep of my friend the Minister of Justice, who adopted it as his own child. Notwithstanding that, whenever a political meeting is held in the province of Quebec many of my opponents still give me credit for that act. Sometimes I am successful and at other times unsuccessful in making them believe that it was the present Minister of Justice, who happens to have the same political views as they themselves, who was responsible for the bill.
It seems to me that the minister should frown upon these amendments which come in from session to session. They are not properly studied, having in mind the general idea of the Bankruptcy Act. The British North America Act permits the federal authorities to legislate upon bankruptcy. The amendments suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver Oentre (Mr. Mackenzie) are amendments which he desires to have put through particularly for his own province, but where the act is a federal act the lawyers practising in different parts .of the country ought to know what the law is ftom the federal point of view. If we have to adopt the particular views and rules governing provincial legislation on bankruptcy, we are back to where we were before 1919. I recognize the fact that in the province of Quebec we have, so to speak, taken the bit in our teeth and incorporated in the federal law our own particular law. But, after all, the laws of the province of Quebec are radically different from those of the other provinces, and it seems to me that the English law governing bankruptcy, upon which this act is based, ought to be satisfactory to all the English-speaking provinces regardless of whether they are in the east or in the west.
I wish to suggest to the Minister of Justice that there should be a general revision of the Bankruptcy Act when everyone interested could appear before a select committee which would deal with the question, and then we

would have some scientific treatment of the whole of the Act. We ought, if I may suggest this to the Minister of Justice, to allow all these bills to amend the Bankruptcy Act at this session) to remain in abeyance, appoint a committee to study the whole matter and then introduce a complete and revised bankruptcy bill which would meet with the views of at least a majority of the people in this country.

I heartily endorse the suggestion made by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie). Wages should take priority over all other claims in a case of bankruptcy. When a firm goes into bankruptcy, probably the last people who know anything about the matter are the workmen in that Concern. Others have their legal representatives, and they are fully apprised of what is about to take place before it actually happens. But the poor workingmen who are in the employ of that firm have no legal representative; they are working in good faith and their wages should have priority over all other claims. Will the Minister of Justice take this point into consideration?

This discussion is hardly appropriate under the proposal that is introduced by this bill. I realize, however, perhaps as well as anyone in the house, the difficulties, the diversities and I might also say some of the anomalies that are met with in the bankruptcy law in this country and its administration in the various provinces. During the short time that I have occupied the position of Minister of Justice, I have received a great many communications from judges, trustees in bankruptcy, receivers in bankruptcy, legal bodies and associations, chambers of commerce, boards of trade, credit men's associations and the like, all suggesting various changes in the Bankruptcy Act. There is a good deal of force in the suggestion made by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) that the time is fast approaching, if it is not already here, when there should be something in the nature of a general revision of the act. Upon the whole, 1 think the public feel that the act has worked well, but there are some difficulties that will have to be smoothed out. It is rather a serious problem to undertake a law for nine provinces where there are provincial jurisdictions which, in many respects, appear to be somewhat conflicting. I have not attempted such a revision during the present session. I have tabulated all the suggestions and all the proposed amendments, and the only amendment which the government has in mind at this session is the present one as incorporated in this measure, to protect in-
jured parties in respect of insurance in regard to motor accidents, accidents either to the person or to the property of others. I am, however, keeping before me the question of a general revision of the ant, and perhaps by next session I may be in a position to introduce such a bill.

Trans-Canada Highway

national issue, because every citizen of this country is directly or indirectly interested in the construction and the routing of this highway. For the sake of discussion I will divide the highway system of Canada into three sections: first the eastern system, comprising Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and parts of Quebec and Ontario; second, the central system, which is the link to be constructed in northern Ontario, and third the western section which will comprise the three prairie provinces and British Columbia. It has been said in the past that the provinces of Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick were not particularly interested in the construction of a trans-Canada highway for the very good reason that the highways of the three provinces are linked up together, but in Quebec we have a different situation. It will be necessary to construct hundreds of miles of new highway from Quebec city towards Cochrane and Winnipeg, and in Ontario we have the same situation. As I stated a few moments ago, in southern Ontario we have the best system of highways not only on the continent but, I was going to say, in the world. In northern Ontario, however, by reason of the size of that section of the province, the sparseness of the population and the lateness of settlement, there exists a situation which. demands the attention not only of the different localities directly interested but of every citizen in the country.
I shall deal briefly with the local situation, but before proceeding to do so I desire to discuss for a moment or two the three highways going westward. I believe the province of Manitoba will have access to the borders of Ontario this year. The province of Saskatchewan has its own highway system east and west, and in Alberta the situation is different from what it is in either Saskatchewan or Manitoba. On the western slope of the Rocky mountains in that province a connecting link of the highway has to be constructed. And the same applies to the province of British Columbia.
Coming back now to the local issue, I trust that the facts I shall place before the house will provoke some discussion. I would make an appeal to all the chambers of commerce in this country because, as I have said, every section of Canada is directly interested in the routing of the highway, particularly so far as northern Ontario is concerned. It is surprising to me that there have not been more pronounced activities on the part of the chambers of commerce of Toronto, Montreal, Halifax, Winnipeg and the other large centres of population. I believe that a solution of
fMr. Bradette.]
the problem will be more quickly arrived at if these larger centres will consider the situation from the point of view of northern Ontario and the whole of Canada.
In northern Ontario the people along the north shore of lake Superior maintain that the trans-Canada highway should go through their section. We contend-and we have logic, distance, and economic considerations on our side-that the highway should parallel the Canadian National railway from La Reine on the Quebec border straight to Winnipeg. But until such time as the people of Canada as a whole undertake to deal with the situation, it will be difficult to find a solution.
At present there are in northern Ontario three schools of thought with regard to the routing of the highway. First of all there are those who favour the north shore routing, which would represent a distance of approximately 585 miles of new road to be constructed. This will run from Sault Ste. Marie to Nipigon, following closely the north shore of lake Superior. Needless to say, the north shore route is backed up by the people all along that section. A distance of 60 miles of road has already been constructed; it extends from the Sault to Batchawana bay. It may be contended by some that, inasmuch as the majority of the population is in the southern section of northern Ontario, the highway should be routed through that section. But we must not overlook the fact that, with development, there will be undoubtedly a much larger population in the northern section in the near future than there is at the present time in the southern section.
There is another school of thought in regard to the routing of the highway. There are those people who believe that the proper route should have the Mississagi valley as its objective. This is a distance of 650 miles of new road to be constructed. I believe that route was first recognized by the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson), and it is sponsored by Chapleau and other towns along the Canadian Pacific railway. It starts some 30 miles east of the Sault and runs north of the Sault and on to Oba. The route connects with the road system and follows the western sections. There is no doubt a3 to the advantages of this route. It would avoid the rocky country and provide a highway system for all the population from North Bay to the Sault. Its construction would be cheaper and it would traverse a section of country rich in wonderful scenery and excellent fishing and one capable of great agricultural development. The important feature of this route is that it provides a basis for

Trans-Canada Highway
compromise between the north and the south. In a resolution I have on the order paper I make allusion to the fact, which is recognized, that eventually alternate routes will have to be constructed; and needless to say, whatever section of northern Ontario has the advantage of the initial route will be at least twenty years ahead of the other. It will take that length of time for the second section to catch up with it.
Then there is the Cochrane or northern route, a distance, from Hearst to Winnipeg, of 519 miles. This will run directly west, and it is a route that will have to be considered. I had some interviews with the premier of Quebec and others living on the western slope of the province. They want to have a direct highway connection with the trans-Canada highway, and the only direct connection that can be afforded will be by way of the Mani-waki road west of the city of Hull and by the Mont Laurier road which will give direct connection with Montreal, going by lake Victoria, and on towards northern Quebec. Such a route will shorten the distance from. Montreal to Winnipeg 150 to 225 miles, and therefore this aspect of the situation must be considered in any discussion of the routing of the trans-Canada highway.
I will now discuss as briefly as I can the merits of the different routes which have been mentioned. I do not wish to be partial, but I need hardly say that, seeing that I belong to the northern section of Ontario, I am naturally in favour of the northern route. I think, however, that I can prove that our section of northern Ontario affords the most favourable facilities for road-making of any section of the country. When I say this I am not casting any reflection on the efforts made in the past by those who have favoured the north shore route. In my opinion, in view of the high cost which would devolve upon the government, and considering the present financial condition of the country, that route must be regarded as impossible. Let me repeat, however, that we in the northern section of the province are willing at all times to come to an honest compromise with other sections of Ontario. We have in that northern part of the province 85 per cent of the entire area of Ontario. We consider, therefore, that we are favourably situated in relation to the route which the highway should take.
Let me discuss the merits of the different routes under five heads:	First, distance;
second, cost; third, possibilities for settlement; fourth, tourist attraction, and fifth, political expediency.
So far as distance is concerned, the northern route is 250 miles shorter, going in the direction of Quebec city, passing Cochrane on the way to Winnipeg. As to cost, I have reliable information from official sources to prove that the cost which the route I advocate would entail, would be less than the others. The northern section of northern Ontario is partly a flat and rolling country, with well forested land and on which there can be found gravel and sand suitable for highway construction; and in from two to four years, at a flat rate of $20,000 per mile, the road could be constructed. This would include cuts, fills, bridges and so forth. It would not make as considerable a demand on the federal treasury as the other routes proposed.
As to the possibilities for settlement, anyone familiar with the situation on the north shore knows that settlement is absolutely impossible in that section of the country, while in the northern section of the province 80 per cent of the land, we know, is capable of settlement-and the settlements in the clay belt are a proof of that statement. As regards attractiveness to tourists, I believe the three routes I have discussed are on a par. The northern section is a paradise for tourists and even at the present time, without means of communication in some sections, we have thousands of visitors from the United States -I had almost said from every part of the world-who go into that part of the country and spend months in the summer and winter time hunting and fishing.
There is one more point to be considered. The statement was made by the chairman of the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario commission that steel will be laid to Moose Factory. Every schoolboy and schoolgirl in Canada and the United States, when looking at the map of the North American continent, sees this great inland waterway called the Hudson Bay, sometimes referred to as the Mediterranean of the North American continent. There is no doubt that every citizen, whether of the United States or Canada, has a desire to visit at least once in his life that wonderful inland sea. The Timiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway will soon have the steel extended as far as Moose Factory, on James bay, the most southerly point on the Hudson bay. The Timiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway is contemplating the building of a large hotel at Moose Factory in order to provide accommodation for the expected tourists, who in my opinion will

I believe it was stated in this house two or three years ago that the geographical division of Canada was a monstrous anomaly, but the people of Canada do not realize the wonderful heritage they have in northern Ontario. We used to think that that section of Canada was practically a barren country, but I repeat that it is really the treasure house of Canada in land, in mines, in water powers, in forests and all kinds of undeveloped resources. A statement was made by Hon. It may surprise some hon. members to know that to us in northern Ontario, Winnipeg, as far as news is concerned, seems as far away as is Russia. I do not desire to prophesy, but I cannot help predicting that within a very short time millions of prosperous contented people will be found in this section of the country. This parliament stands before the tribunal of public opinion to see to it that we be given what was promised last July.

Let me quote the Sudbury Star of September 17, 1930:
The benefits accruing to a municipality through having an aggressive board of trade have been aptly demonstrated in the vital question of the construction of the proposed trans-Canada highway, which has been agitating the northern Ontario centres during the last few weeks, and which is one of the most important problems affecting the vast stretch of country north of the Canadian Pacific Railway that has been in the public mind for a long time.
Without a board of trade, it is doubtful if any active steps would be officially taken in a matter of this kind. The project does not come within the province of a municipal council, although, if the latter were not over-occupied in purely civic problems, they might, in a measure, divert their attention to through roads.
He proceeds to explain the necessity of a trans-Canada highway. I rise on this occasion just to add a few words to what has already been said by the hon. member for North Timiskaming (Mr. Bradette). I want especially to emphasize that if we ask, regardless of partisan views, for the immediate construction of this trans-Canada highway, it is to relieve the unemployment situation which is so bad at the present time. In my constituency unemployment is becoming worse every week. I want to mention in particular the town of Sturgeon Falls, with a population of 4,000 which for twenty-five years has depended for its livelihood on the operations of the Spanish River pulp industry which is now the Abitibi Pulp and Paper Company. This company, however, closed its doors seven or eight months ago. Charitable contributions have reached their limit; the municipality can do no more; the provincial contributions have also reached their limit, and now it is the federal government's turn to step in and do something. Therefore I ask for the construction of this trans-Can-,-ada highway, mostly for the relief of the un-[DOT]employment situation. I might congratulate ;the municipalities and the provincial government for having tried last fall to do something to relieve the unemployment situation. But what has been d'one for the relief of

unemployment, in the district of Sudbury, particularly around Malttawa and Sturgeon Falls has been altogether impractical, and the methods which have been adopted were far from being profitable for the country. Large pieces of road have been built in the middle of winter whereas in the spring the same work could have 'been done in one-tenth of the time with one-quarter of the money. It is my opinion that such work should have been begun early test spring, because at such time it could have been done much more advantageously.
I have a further reason for suggesting the immediate construction of the trans-Canada highway, because the expense involved would be well justified. To my mind such construction would constitute a good piece of business. Referring to the tourist trade in Canada the Ottawa Journal of May 22, 1931, contains the following report:
In 1930 almost five and a half million United States automobiles crossed into Canada, and both Ottawa and Washington estimate that in the neighbourhood of $400,000,000 was put into circulation in the dominion as a result.
Northern Ontario being a more undeveloped country, needs such a road for its further development, and at the same time that section of the oountry would receive its fair share of the tourist trade. Up to the present time many of the Canadian people have been under the impression that American tourists have come to Canada simply to quench their thirst. I think that is an erroneous view; the vast majority of tourists enter Canada to enjoy the beauties of our country. Undoubtedly a great many of them would be drawn to northern Ontario if the road now under discussion was built. Northern Ontario would share to. a considerable extent in the $400,000,000 referred to in the Ottawa Journal.
I shall not add anything further about the necessity for the construction of the trans-Cafiada highway, but would strongly urge the government to consider the matter and to take action immediately. The construction of such a highway is a vast undertaking and before it could be undertaken engineers would have to survey the whole rouite, which undoubtedly would involve a work lasting some weeks and probably months. If the route is not now decided upon, construction work may not be initiated this year. I hope the government will take immedia te steps to decide upon a rouite, have it surveyed and give work to thousands of men as was promised during the election campaign.

Trans-Canada Highway

My hon. friend
is undoubtedly aware that two or three routes have been suggested. Which of these routes would he favour?

The different routes
have been outlined by the hon. member for North Timiskaming (Mr. Bradette). Naturally every one would like to see the road pass through his own home town. The hon. member for North Timiskaming urged that the road should pass through his district, and similarly I wish to have it pass through mine; but I have no hesitation in saying that hon. members on this side of the house are above politics in ithe matter and will leave the routing to the decision of the provincial and federal governments. We would accept their decision gladly and would like to see the work proceed immediately.

I would like to add to the remarks
of the hon. members for North Timiskaming and Nipissing concerning the construction of a trans-Canada highway. Owing to the fact that the government has definitely promised to build a national highway I am disappointed that we have not heard some pronouncement concerning its construction. Undoubtedly during the last election campaign the present administration made definite promises with respect to the building of a highway through northern Ontario. The hon. member for Nippissing has referred to a statement made by the Minister of Lands and Forests for Ontario at a smoker held in the town of Sudbury during the last election campaign wherein he stated that the highway now under discussion was a federal obligation. The St. John Telegraph-Journal of July 1, 1930, contained the following statement made by the present Prime Minister at St. John, New Brunswick:
We say that the federal government under our administration will build a great national highway in Canada.
No statement could be more definite than that.
The London Free Press of June 25, 1930, contains the following statement made by the Prime Minister at Cobourg on the preceding day:
"A national highway for Canadians. A highway in Canada, not through some other country. A highway in which you can leave Cape Breton and arrive in Vancouver without going into any foreign land." Mr. Bennett declared that the undertaking must be accomplished by the hands of the federal government.
To my' mind that statement regarding the building of a national highway is quite definite.
The Ottawa Morning Citizen, in an issue the date of which I have not been able to ascertain, published the following extract from a speech delivered by the present Prime Minister at Ormsitown:
A national highway was required for agriculture, to connect the east with the west; to this national highway his party was pledged.
I could refer to many other quotations of a similar character, but I do not think I should burden hon. members. Undoubtedly they are fully seized of the fact that the Conservative party, the Prime Minister in particular, placed themselves definitely on record during the last election campaign to the effect that a national highway would be built at the instance of the federal government. I think a definite pronouncement should be made to ease the anxiety of the people of northern Ontario as to whether or not the federal government is going to build or assist the provinces in building a national highway. An announcement to that effect has not been made by the present administration.
I spoke on this matter at some length in the course of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and I do not propose at this time to repeat what I then said. But I think it is well that we should ask the government to make some definite announcement which would at least put an end to the anxiety of the people and also stop the political manoeuvering of a few persons in northern Ontario who have delayed the building of the highway for so many years. I think probably a brief history of the highway might be useful in order to enlighten some members of the house who may be interested in it.
My official connection with it commenced in the town of Dryden in 1919 when I became a member of the Ontario legislature. At that time delegates from every town and hamlet between Winnipeg to away east of the head of the lakes met and formed an organization known as the Central Canada Colonization and Highway Association. The president of the association was, and is to-day, a leading Conservative in northern Ontario. In fact he was the defeated candidate in the provincial election of 1919. If I took the time of the house to read the names of the officers of the association, hon. members would realize that most of them are leading Conservatives
Trans-Canada Highway

in that section of the country. So this was not a political organization in any sense. The executive met, formulated a memorial and presented it to the Ontario government in March, 1920. A couple of paragraphs will indicate what the association had in mind at that particular time. After declaring that Ontario should construct the highway piece by piece the memorial proceeds:
The Manitoba government is prepared to complete its portion of the road just as soon as the Ontario government defines the meeting place, and the Manitoba engineers are waiting to do the work in conjunction with your engineers. The necessity of this point being defined is important, and if this has not already been done, we trust that you will immediately take steps to have it completed.
It will be observed that members of the association had already met the Manitoba government and had received an assurance from them that they were prepared to do their part of the work. The memorial proceeds by resolution:
That this executive is of the opinion that the Ontario government should map out its road building program so that the Winnipeg to head of the lakes highway be completed within five years, and that, during 1920 the road from Kenora to the Manitoba boundary should be completed, also 42 miles of road from the head of the lakes be provided by the building of 34 miles of new road and the gravelling of 13 miles.
The memorial further says:
We, therefore, ask that during the year 1920 the provincial government in Ontario complete the work as outlined in resolution No. 1 hereinbefore.
That was the attitude of the people in the portion of the territory in which I reside. Mr. Pitt of Dryden, as president, presented that memorial to the Ontario government in March 1920. Work was started and got fairly under way, and, as requested, there was a survey made from Kenora to the Manitoba boundary, the right of way was cut and grubbed and some grading done. In 1923, as we well know, there was a change of government in Ontario, and thereupon the work, for some reason or other was practically shut down. We urged on the new government of Ontario the desirability of carrying on the work that had been started in 1921, and we find the Hon. James Lyons, stating at the head of the lakes, as reported in the Fort William Times-Journal of May 30, 1924:
Completed in three years. The policy of the government is to open up northern Ontario roads as speedily as possible. The highway through to the Manitoba boundary will be a direct line from Fort William north of Rainy River and Fort Frances and will be completed

within three years. The road eastward towards the Soo will be undertaken at once, and will be completed within the next seven years, it is hoped. Not only will engineers be on the route, but work will be commenced within a few days.
I have read sufficient to show that a very definite pledge was made to proceed with the construction. Notwithstanding that pledge nothing was done, and as a matter of fact the road is still uncompleted. At that time we had other highways under consideration, and surveyors were blazing a trail across from the Canadian Pacific Railway to the town of Sioux Lookout, but that work, too, was suspended. In answer to a letter of mine the Hon. James W. Lyons, then, Minister of Lands and Forests, wrote me under date of March 4, 1924:
Your letter of March 3rd, with petition regarding the Canadian Pacific Railway Sioux Lookout road received, and have to advise that this matter will be given consideration along with the other real needs of the north, but it will probably be the first to the middle of April before any decision is made in the matter.
That is a road that connects up with the main highway we are now discussing. Every conceivable excuse was made by the Ontario government for not proceeding with the highway. At one time they stated that the Manitoba government had not put itself on record as willing to meet the Ontario government at any particular point; but I myself accompanied a delegation to Winnipeg along with the president of the association that I have referred to and, Colonel Schnarr, president of the board of trade of Kenora, and others and in conjunction with members of the Manitoba legislature we secured a definite promise from their government to meet the Ontario government at mile post 24. In addition, before the Bracken government came into power we had Mr. McPherson put h:s government on record in the matter in a letter to the mayor of Keewatin, and no doubt this will be of interest to some hon. members. This letter is from the office of the Minister of Public Works, Winnipeg, under date of August 10, 1921, addressed to N. J. Hansen, mayor of' Keewatin, Ontario.
Re: Ontario-Manitoba Highway Hear Sir:
1 beg to acknowledge receipt of your communication dated August 8th inquiring as to the location of the connecting proposed route of the Manitoba-Ontario highway at the Ontario border.
I have had this matter under consideration for some time, and after due consideration and consultation with our reclamation branch it is agreed that the vicinity of mile post 24, or in other words at or about mile post 24, will be satisfactory from the standpoint of this province.

Trans-Canada Highway
I trust that this will meet the requirements of the situation at the present time, and as I understand the Ontario Minister of Lands, Hon, Mr. Bowman, is to visit your district very shortly, this will be in the nature of an assurance as to the location of the proposed road.
I am in receipt of correspondence from Mr. Wydeman, of the Kenora Examiner and Mr. Cornish of the Canada Colonization and Highway Association, and copies of this letter are being forwarded to each of these gentlemen.
Yours faithfully,
C. T>. McPherson, Minister of Public Works.
So there was no doubt in our minds that there was a definite arrangement between the two governments to meet at mile post 24. Indeed, in 1926, one of the Conservative candidates for the provincial house, Mr. J. P. Eamgey, issued a statement to the electors in which he said:-
If elected, I propose to join forces with the members for Rainy River, Fort William and Port Arthur for the rapid completion of the portion of the trans-Canada highway from Fort William west; and for the construction at once of the highway to Fort Frances to tap at that point the great tourist traffic from the United States which is waiting to flow this way.
So the government candidate had no thought whatever that this highway would be built only on condition that the federal government contributed anything to it. As a matter of fact, until the approach of the last federal election there never was a suggestion from any point that the federal government should contribute one red cent to the cost of the construction of that highway through that portion of the country. Mayor Webb of Winnipeg, a very pronounced Conservative, took issue with a Liberal during the campaign of 1926, and in a letter to the Fort Frances Times under date of August 26, 1926, he said:
We must all work together and the man or women or any political party or any organization that in any way, shape or form, tries to create or breed friction, deserve to be shown by the people at large that they will have nothing to do with them whatsoever.
Neither of the parties at Ottawa have anything to do with the local problem of a highway between Winnipeg and Kenora, or in the great development of this wonderful area.
So here we have a very pronounced Conservative taking a Liberal to task because he suggested a federal contribution. Of course it is true that Mayor Webb changed his views during the last election and joined with a good many others in misrepresenting the position of the Liberals, and particularly my own position, in connection with the trans-Canada highway.
A few moments ago I quoted Mr. Lyons, who was Minister of Lands and Forests in
1924. As hon. members will recall, Mr. Lyons resigned and was succeeded by Mr. Finlayson. In the Kenora Examiner of September 16, 1927, we have this statement by Mr. Finlayson:
The government propose, after the completion of the Ferguson highway, this year, to devote more money and attention to the roads in the northwestern part of the province. The development from Port Arthur and Fort William to the Manitoba boundary requires attention, and during the next year or two the roads in this section of the province call for very considerable improvement.
Then we have ex-Mayor Toole, of Kenora, another very pronounced Conservative-and in passing I might say one of the most decent Conservatives in northern Ontario-speaking at a banquet in honour of Mr. Finlayson at Kenora. Mr. Toole was selected to present to Mr. Finlayson the views of the people in that part of the country with respect to many matters. In connection with the highway, I find the following comment, in the Kenora Examiner of August 26, 1927:
Why can we not have a road to Dryden? Why should we not be connected up with that part of our own district? Only about forty-five miles of construction are needed to link us up to that thriving agricultural section who need the road as much as we. Dryden and Kenora, two good towns, and many smaller communities cut off from each other. Hon. James Lyons, on a visit some years ago, promised it; yet the road is not built.
You have said that a road from the south would bring in foreign wealth, not only tourists but some ready to invest as well. Much of the country around Toronto itself was built up by visitors who were quick to see an opportunity. Money expended on highways here will bring enough tourists to give returns that not only pay for maintenance but construction as well.
The automobile has revolutionized everything in the last few years. We hear of roads being built all around us, but so far only twenty-two miles has been built for Kenora. We in this district are loyal to Ontario, but to-day unfortunately there is much dissatisfaction against the government for the lack of progress in this section.
Those are the words of one of the leading Conservatives of that section of the country. Anyone who knows Mr. Toole will agree that he is one of the most far-seeing gentlemen in northern Ontario, and a man who is always boosting his district. Then we had the president of the Central Canada Highways Association, Mr. Alfred Pitt, who was invited to address the Kenora Rotary Club. He is reported in the Kenora Examiner of November 30, 1928, as follows:
Well, we spent a good deal of time and money, and finally Mr. Lyons started what now is the road to within twelve miles of the Manitoba boundary.
Trans-Canada Highway

Of course, he is wrong in that statement; that road was started before Mt. Lyons was Minister of Lands and Forests.
And so soon are things forgotten, I have heard it claimed that Ontario and Manitoba had not agreed upon a meeting place. This is not so. The surveyors of the two provinces did not meet with the precision of the Simplon tunnel, but came within measurable distance of each other. There need be no difficulty here. The point is settled, although some newspapers, not going editorially deep enough into the facts, seem to forget that.
So that we have Mr. Pitt almost despairing of the possibility of getting this highway, and taking some of the editorial writers in that part of the country to task. I am sure I do not need to mention who they are. One particular gentleman who was a candidate- in fact, he was the legislative representative in Ontario-never writes an editorial on the highway, lately at least, without misrepresenting the whole situation. And that, I may say, is one of the reasons why to-day he is not a member of the Ontario legislature for that riding.
I shall read presently an extract from the Dryden Observer of July 17, 1930. Apparently the whole aspect of this matter has changed. Every speaker in the Conservative ranks taking part in the election campaign in northern Ontario-this was particularly the case in my own riding-endeavoured to misrepresent my position. I have the records of their statements. The whole aspect of the situation, I say, has changed. In the campaign it was no longer a provincial undertaking. Even some of the gentlemen whom I have quoted, who had stated that it was a provincial undertaking with which the federal government had nothing to do, whether that government was Liberal or Conservative, took a different attitude in 1930, declaring then that it was a dominion undertaking. These gentlemen changed their opinion, saying that it was a federal obligation and that the highway would never be constructed until there was a change of government at Ottawa. Let me quote from a writer in the Dryden Observer of July 17, 1930:
Premier Howard G. Ferguson, in his effort to make political capital in the present compaign, tells us he is ready to go fifty-fifty with the federal government in the cost of construction of the highway in this riding, and he and his henchmen, among them Hon. Wm. Finlayson, who was here recently, attack the King administration for not accepting this offer and permitting the work to proceed, thereby affording employment. Manitoba, the prairie provinces and British Columbia each went ahead with their sections and completed . them without delay. But Premier Ferguson holds out for fifty-fifty split.

I placed on the order paper a motion which was carried by the house, asking for the correspondence between the government of Ontario and any member of the federal government; and while there were returns from every department of the federal government, there was not one syllable, not one line of communication as between the two governments indicating any request for assistance or for a fifty-fifty split.
The election was fought in our part of the country chiefly on the highways. The Conservatives gained two seats in that part of the country mainly on the promise of that highway, and I am glad now to be in a position to supplement what was said by the hon. member for N'orth Timiskaming (Mr. Bradetite), and the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Hurtubise). With those hon. gentlemen, I would ask the government to implement their promise and to do so immediately. It is a shame to think that in a beautiful country such as we have in northern Ontario we should be denied a highway to enable the people to Communicate with the rest of the world. Moreover, ithere are people outside looking for scenic beauty, a lovely country such as we have there, with delightful lakes, forests, fishing and game of all kinds. These people are anxious to spend some of their money there and they cannot because of the political manoeuvering of about six gentlemen or so up in my part of the country. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, in view of the definite pledge made by the Conservatives in my riding during the campaign, and the different promises, as I have outlined them, made by the present Prime Minister, that the government should make some pronouncement as to whether or not they intend to carry out these promises. They should let us know whether they are going to proceed with the construction of that highway as they pledged themselves to do or whether they have changed their minds and intend to make a contribution to the provinces by way of assistance. Whatever course they follow, whether by contribution to the provinces or by undertaking the whole thing themselves, they will have my support.
As regards the route from the head of the lakes to the Manitoba boundary, the question is settled as to the roulte. The people themselves have agreed upon the routte and have so represented to the Ontario government. Whether they sent copies to this government, I do not know. But the present federal government ought not now to seek further excuses on the ground that there are representations from different parts of fbe country

with regard to the question of route. No matter what representations are made, the government is responsible to the people for the route they should tlake, and I would suggest that they shoulder that responsibility and establish the route. I am satisfied that if they did so the people in northern Ontario would get behind them and accept whatever route they selected.
While speaking of routes, there is no doubt in .my mind that before many years there will be demand's for more highways than one in northern Ontario. I am satisfied that if the route should go north the people in the other section of the country will feel that there should be another route; similarly, if the highway is built in the south there will be required before long a northern route. We have two or three routes from the city of Toronto to Hamilton. All through old Ontario you can choose various routes wherever you want to go, and these highways have been built in large part out of the revenues provided by new Ontario. The revenues from mining, fishing, game, forests and water-powers have all contributed to the building of these highways through old Ontario, and I was very much surprised during the last provincial by-election to read that Mr. Mc-Crea, a gentleman who I am sure knows what he is talking about, made the statement that, at this very moment, for every dollar the Ontario government places in northern Ontario it get back ten dollars. If that is true -I do not happen to have his speech here, but I can get it-that is all the more reason why more consideration should be given to the north than it is receiving at the present time. And even if it is noit true, the province of Ontario and this government, now that it is under obligation to carry out its promise in this regard, should give greater assistance to that sparsely settled country in accordance with their pledges.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. J. COWAN (Port Arthur-Thunder Bay):
speechtext:
I wish to intervene in this debate
for a few moments inasmuch as the route of the trans-Canada highway would of necessity pass through the district I have the honour to represent. The members of the government, particulary those from northern Ontario, in the past have been in favour of the construction of a trans-Canada highway and at all times have endeavoured to promote the possibility of having that route constructed as early as possible. I do not think there is any argument as to the advisability of the construction and the early commencement of it. Confederation became possible because of the construction of a
trans-Canada railway, and in the world of transportation the motor has become a very important item. It would seem to me that the unity of Canada would be promoted if a motor road were constructed across this country, and particularly is that true of northern Ontario.
I do not propose to discuss this issue at great length, except to say that in the communities of northern Ontario we have not a municipal organization. There are no township or county organizations which would contribute towards the cost of this highway, it must be borne either by the provincial or by the federal governments, or by both. It is a matter which can be discussed properly in this parliament; it is a national matter, and for that reason I say that the government now in power should give it its earnest consideration.
Knowing the attitude which this government and the members of the cabinet have taken in the past, I have no hesitation in saying that this is one policy which should be carried ou.t very shortly.
